-# Gramaire site
-
-The Astro + Starlight site for Gramaire, rebuilt to the Claude Design mock
-("Gramaire branding enhancement"). The brand tokens, the live editor, and the
-Lab all run the **real** compiled Scala engine — never a stand-in.
-
-## Structure
-
-- **Home (`/`)** — a standalone splash, [src/pages/index.astro](src/pages/index.astro):
-  hero, the live "one file · edit the source" showcase, capability tiles.
-  Outside Starlight's chrome, so it defines its own theme bootstrap.
-- **Lab (`/lab`)** — [src/pages/lab.astro](src/pages/lab.astro): the mock's
-  app-shell playground (draggable split editor + ten-tab analysis drawer +
-  status strip), every tab backed by a real `gramaire.Playground` field.
-- **Docs / Specs / Tutorials** — Starlight content under
-  [src/content/docs/](src/content/docs/); the brand favicon and split-stem
-  wordmark come from the config and the `SiteTitle` override.
-- **Shared** — [LiveGrammar.astro](src/components/LiveGrammar.astro) (the
-  framework-free live-edit island embedded on the landing, tutorial, and
-  docs) and the Scala.js `site-glue` module
-  ([../site-glue/js/src/main/scala/gramaire/site/](../site-glue/js/src/main/scala/gramaire/site/)),
-  bundled to `src/generated/site-glue.mjs`: `GramaireRuntime` (the engine
-  wrapper), `Diagrams` (the railroad renderer, sharing `gramaire.Railroad`
-  with the CLI's `gramaire fmt`), and `LabLink` (the private-by-hash
-  Open-in-Lab deep-link codec).
-
-## Develop locally
-
-```sh
-cd site
-npm install
-npm run build:engine      # bundle the Scala core → src/generated/gramaire-engine.mjs
-npm run build:site-glue   # bundle the site's Scala.js logic → src/generated/{site-glue,engine-worker}.mjs
-npm run dev
-```
-
-## Build & test
-
-```sh
-cd site
-npm run build             # static site → dist/
-npm test                  # engine + view-helper suite (tsx), against the compiled site-glue bundle
-npm run lint               # prettier --check
-npm run check:engine      # regenerate the engine bundle and assert it matches its source
-npm run check:site-glue   # regenerate the site-glue/engine-worker bundles and assert they match
-```
-
-## The generated bundles
-
-- `src/generated/gramaire-engine.mjs` — `npm run build:engine`
-  (`sbt playground/fullLinkJS` over `gramaire.playground.Main`). The thin
-  `evaluate()` entry point: the same filesystem-free compiler core the
-  `gramaire` CLI runs.
-- `src/generated/site-glue.mjs` / `engine-worker.mjs` — `npm run build:site-glue`
-  (`sbt siteGlue/fullLinkJS engineWorker/fullLinkJS`). The site's own logic
-  (diagrams, FIRST/FOLLOW, CST views, Open-in-Lab links, the off-thread parse
-  worker), ported from TypeScript to Scala.js.
-
-All three are committed so the site builds without an sbt/Scala toolchain;
-regenerate them whenever the corresponding Scala sources change, and keep
-`gramaire-engine.d.ts` / `site-glue.d.ts` in sync.
-
-## Publish to GitHub Pages
-
-The GitHub Actions workflow in
-[.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml](../.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml)
-publishes the generated site from `site/dist` on pushes to `develop`.

-export const glossary: Record<string, string> = {
-  recognizer:
-    "A parser that only answers yes/no — does the input fit the grammar? — without building a value or a tree.",
-  nonterminal:
-    "A named grammar rule (mixed-case in Gramaire), defined by its productions. Contrast a terminal.",
-  terminal:
-    "A literal piece of input — a quoted spelling like '+', or a token class like NUMBER.",
-  "token-class":
-    "An ALL-CAPS lexer rule (e.g. NUMBER : /[0-9]+/) that matches a family of input text, not one fixed spelling.",
-  "shift-reduce":

-  "lalr-artifact":

-  cst: "Concrete syntax tree: every token and rule the parser matched, brackets and operators included.",

@@ -1,236 +0,0 @@
----
-title: Language Specification
-description: The formal Gramaire grammar format — document envelope, lexical rules, newline normalization, desugaring, and the IR/CST contracts.
----
-
-import { Aside } from "@astrojs/starlight/components";
-
-This is the formal definition of the Gramaire grammar language (v0.1): the
-document envelope, the `lr` lexical grammar, the newline rule, the desugaring
-that compiles surface sugar to the epsilon-free core, and the contracts the
-compiler emits. Keywords MUST / SHOULD / MAY per RFC 2119.
-
-<Aside>
-  The canonical on-disk layout that `gramaire fmt` produces is specified
-  separately in the [fmt output
-  contract](../../../../../docs/fmt-output-contract.md). This page specifies the
-  _language_; that one specifies its _formatting_.
-</Aside>
-
-## 1. Document envelope
-
-A Gramaire grammar is hosted in a GitHub-Flavored Markdown document. The compiler
-ignores prose, list markers, and images; it extracts the grammar by scanning ATX
-headings and fenced code blocks whose info string begins with `gramaire`.
-
-- **Grammar name.** The single `# H1`. There MUST be exactly one.
-- **Nonterminal rules.** Every non-reserved `## H2` names a nonterminal; the
-  `lr` block beneath it holds that rule's productions.
-- **Reserved `## H2` sections.** `General settings` (a `gramaire settings` block
-  of document-level directives — currently `%lang <host>`, which declares the
-  language of inline `{% … %}` actions), `Precedence` (an `lr precedence` block),
-  `Error messages` (an `lr errors` block), and `Generated tables` (the emitted
-  FIRST/FOLLOW table). They appear in that order when present.
-- **Presentational headings.** `###` and deeper headings carry no structural
-  meaning; they are free grouping the analyzer skips. Only the H1 and H2 layers
-  are structural.
-- **One grammar per file.** A file defines exactly one start symbol and one
-  nonterminal namespace. Reuse across files is a future cross-file `import`,
-  never in-file sub-grammars or multiple H1s.
-
-## 2. Lexical grammar of an `lr` block
-
-Inside an `lr` productions block the lexer emits these token classes:
-
-| Token                     | Form                     | Meaning                                              |
-| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
-| `IDENT`                   | `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` | a nonterminal (mixed-case) or token class (ALL-CAPS) |
-| `TERM_LIT`                | `` `…` ``                | a backtick-delimited literal terminal                |
-| `:` / `\|`                | `:` / `\|`               | rule-head colon / alternative separator              |
-| `ACTION`                  | `{% … %}`                | a semantic action; body kept verbatim                |
-| `LABEL`                   | `# Name`                 | an alternative label (visitor / accessor name)       |
-| `ATTR`                    | `#[name]`                | a rule attribute (e.g. `#[inline]`)                  |
-| `PLUS` `STAR` `QUESTION`  | `+` `*` `?`              | repetition / optional postfixes                      |
-| `LANGLE` `RANGLE` `COMMA` | `<` `>` `,`              | macro-call punctuation                               |
-| `NL`                      | one or more line breaks  | structural newline (see §3)                          |
-
-A name is a **nonterminal** exactly when it appears as some rule's left-hand
-side; any other mixed-case name referenced but never defined is a build error
-(not a silent terminal). An ALL-CAPS name is always a token class. Input
-tokenization itself is per-language: the `lr` lexer reads the grammar; a separate
-lexer turns _input_ strings into tokens whose `terminal` names match the
-grammar's terminals.
-
-## 3. Newline normalization (Option A)
-
-A line break **inside an alternative is insignificant** — `|` is the only
-alternative separator, so a long alternative may wrap across physical lines. Only
-two newlines are structural, and a normalization pass keeps exactly those before
-the parser runs:
-
-- the **head** `NL` inside `IDENT NL :` (or `ATTR IDENT NL :`), which is what
-  distinguishes a rule head from a same-line `name:Sym` field (`IDENT : Sym`);
-  and
-- the **boundary** `NL` immediately before the next head.
-
-Every other newline — between two symbols, before a `|`, before a label or
-action, at a block edge — is dropped. The lookahead that classifies a newline
-happens once, in this pass, so the grammar stays LR(1) on one token of lookahead
-with no `;` terminators.
-
-<Aside type="caution">
-  A consequence: a `name:Sym` field MUST stay on one line. Splitting it across a
-  break reads the name as a rule head.
-</Aside>
-
-## 4. Desugaring to the epsilon-free core
-
-Before building tables, the surface grammar is lowered to a pure, epsilon-free
-context-free grammar. The core automaton never sees a nullable rule, which keeps
-table construction free of nullable bookkeeping.
-
-### 4.1 Repetition — `X+`, `X*`
-
-`X+` (one-or-more) lowers to a fresh left-recursive list nonterminal whose action
-accumulates an `Array`:
-
-```text
-X_plus
-  : X
-  | X_plus X
-```
-
-`X*` (zero-or-more) reuses that list but enumerates **present / absent** at the
-use site, so the empty case is a real production rather than an epsilon — the
-core stays epsilon-free.
-
-### 4.2 Optional — `X?`
-
-`X?` desugars by **use-site enumeration with generated wrapper actions**. A rule
-`A : pre X? post {% f %}` becomes two epsilon-free productions:
-
-```text
-A : pre X post   -- wrapper applies f with (Just x)
-A : pre post     -- wrapper applies f with Nothing
-```
-
-The wrapper splices the original action verbatim, so it still receives one
-`Maybe` and arity is preserved. With _k_ optionals an alternative enumerates to
-2^k productions; an all-optional alternative (which would enumerate to an empty
-production) is a build error, never a silent epsilon.
-
-### 4.3 Macros — `Comma<X>`, `Sep<X, S>`
-
-`Comma<X>` and `Sep<X, S>` lower to a fresh one-or-more separated-list rule
-(separated by `,` or by the given symbol `S`). An unknown macro or wrong arity is
-a build error.
-
-### 4.4 Named fields — `name:X`
-
-A `name:X` prefix names that right-hand position. The name is carried onto the
-IR's `rhs[].field` and feeds CST accessors and generated visitors; it does not
-change the recognized language. A bare-body action then binds the field
-names: a production `left:NUM '+' right:NUM {% Add left right %}` rewrites
-to `\left _ right -> Add left right`.
-
-Under `%lang javascript`, an action instead receives its children as a single
-**namedtuple** `c` — an array read by index (`c[0]`, `c[2]`) or, for a named
-position, by field (`c.left`) or destructuring (`({ left, right }) => …`). The
-field names are the same `rhs[].field` entries.
-
-A position with **no** explicit `name:` is still auto-named by its symbol
-(`Expr` → `c.expr`, a token class lowercased) — but **only when that symbol occurs
-once** among the rule's nameable positions (nonterminals and token classes;
-literals are never named). A repeated symbol (`Expr '+' Expr`) or a name that
-would collide with an explicit field stays index-only, with no silent
-disambiguation. Auto-naming is a codegen convenience; it does not alter the IR.
-
-### 4.5 Inline folding — `#[inline]`
-
-`#[inline]` marks a single-production rule to be folded into every use site and
-then dropped — both a DRY tool and a way to hand-fit a grammar into LR(1). When
-the using alternative has an action, the inline rule's own action is threaded
-through a wrapper so values still flow.
-
-### 4.6 Labels — `# Name`
-
-A `# Name` label names an alternative. It surfaces in the IR as an optional
-`rules[].label` and drives per-alternative visitor method names and CST accessors.
-
-For a host-agnostic AST, **prefer labels over inline `{% … %}` actions** (ADR
-D37). A label like `# MulDiv` generates a typed `MulDiv(children)` method on the
-emitted `Visitor<T>` — exactly ANTLR's `visitMulDiv` pattern — that you implement
-in any target. Inline actions, by contrast, are host source: the `%lang`
-directive declares their language, so a grammar that carries them is tied to that
-host (e.g. `%lang javascript` bakes a self-contained `evaluate(cst)`). So:
-
-```gramaire
-expr
-  : expr '*' term   # MulDiv
-  | expr '+' term   # AddSub
-  | NUM             # Int
-```
-
-emits `interface Visitor<T> { MulDiv(c): T; AddSub(c): T; Int(c): T; … }` — you
-fill in the methods in your host language, no inline lambda required. Inline
-`{% … %}` stays available for one-liners where a visitor class is overkill.
-
-## 5. The IR contract — `gramaire-ir`
-
-The compiler emits the analyzed grammar and its parse tables as a versioned JSON
-document, the [IR schema](../ir-schema/). Every backend reads only this artifact —
-isolating target generators from Markdown processing and layout entirely.
-
-```json
-{
-  "irVersion": 0,
-  "grammar": {
-    "name": "Calc",
-    "start": "Expr",
-    "rules": [
-      {
-        "id": 0,
-        "lhs": 0,
-        "rhs": [
-          { "id": 0, "kind": "nonterminal", "field": "left" },
-          { "id": 2, "kind": "terminal" },
-          { "id": 1, "kind": "nonterminal", "field": "right" }
-        ],
-        "label": "Add",
-        "actions": [["default", "\\l _ r -> Add l r"]]
-      }
-    ]
-  },
-  "tables": {
-    "algorithm": "canonical",
-    "stateCount": 42,
-    "action": [],
-    "goto": []
-  },
-  "conflicts": []
-}
-```
-
-## 6. The CST contract — `gramaire-cst`
-
-An action-free grammar still fully defines a **concrete syntax tree**: a `branch`
-per reduced production (tagged with its `rules[]` index) and a `token` leaf per
-consumed terminal, children in source order. This generic tree is the portable
-artifact any backend can emit and any host can walk; its shape is fixed by the
-[CST schema](../cst-schema/). The spanned tokenizer carries exact source ranges,
-so a tool can link a CST node back to both its production and its input slice —
-the substrate the [Lab](/gramaire/lab) uses for hover-linking.
-
-## 7. Table construction and conflicts
-
-Tables build by canonical **LR(1)**, **LALR(1)** (canonical states merged by
-LR(0) core), or **IELR(1)** (LALR with the conflicting merges split apart).
-Canonical is the most powerful and serves as the differential oracle for the
-other two.
-
-A conflict is reported in grammar terms — naming the competing productions, not a
-state number — and classified by comparing the three methods: a conflict LALR(1)
-reports but canonical / IELR resolve is an **LALR artifact** (build with IELR);
-one that survives canonical LR(1) is **genuine** (the grammar is ambiguous or not
-LR(1)). For genuinely ambiguous grammars the GLR engine returns the full parse
-forest — every derivation of the input.

-title: Getting Started
-description: Write your first self-rendering grammar — from Markdown structure to a live parse — in about ten minutes.
----
-
-import {
-  Aside,
-  Steps,
-  Card,
-  CardGrid,
-  LinkCard,
-} from "@astrojs/starlight/components";
-import Term from "../../../components/Term.astro";
-import LiveGrammar from "../../../components/LiveGrammar.astro";
-import OpenInLab from "../../../components/OpenInLab.astro";
-import RuleDiagram from "../../../components/RuleDiagram.astro";
-import {
-  DIGIT,
-  CALC,
-  getDefaultGrammar,
-} from "../../../generated/site-glue.mjs";
-
-Gramaire's whole idea is in its name — _gram + mark_, grammar plus Markdown. A
-`.gram.md` file is a normal Markdown document that renders on GitHub — prose,
-railroad diagrams, FIRST/FOLLOW tables — and is **at the same time** the exact
-input the parser generator reads. Your grammar _is_ your documentation.
-
-This tutorial builds a small calculator grammar in two passes: **Part 1** writes
-a <Term name="recognizer">recognizer</Term> that decides whether input is valid,
-and **Part 2** attaches _actions_ that turn a valid parse into a value. The `gramaire` CLI and the
-[Lab](/gramaire/lab) run the **same** Scala core — the Lab is that core
-compiled to Scala.js as browser-native ES modules — so a verdict in the
-browser matches the CLI.
-
-<Aside type="tip" title="The Lab runs the real engine">
-  The browser Lab is not a stub: it bundles the compiled Gramaire core and lexes
-  input from a grammar's literal terminals **and** its token classes (ALL-CAPS
-  names like `NUMBER`, declared as `NUMBER : /[0-9]+/`), then parses with the LR
-  tables — entirely client-side, with no server round-trip. Your grammar never
-  leaves the page.
-</Aside>
-
-## 1. The shape of a `.gram.md` file
-
-A grammar file is a canonical Markdown document with a fixed structure:
-
-<Steps>
-
-1. **One `# H1`** — the grammar's name.
-
-2. **One `## H2` per nonterminal** — the heading names the rule; a `gramaire`
-   fenced block under it holds its productions.
-
-3. **Reserved `## H2` sections** — `Precedence`, `Error messages`, and
-   `Generated tables`, in that order, when present.
-
-4. **Everything else is prose** — paragraphs, images, and `###`+ headings are
-   free presentational grouping the compiler ignores.
-
-</Steps>
-
-One file is exactly one grammar: one start symbol, one namespace. Productions
-live in fenced blocks whose info string is `gramaire`; everything outside them is
-documentation that travels with the grammar.
-
-## 2. Your first rule
-
-Create `calc.gram.md` and give it a title and a first nonterminal:
-
-````md
-# Calc
-
-A small arithmetic grammar.
-
-## Expr
-
-An expression is a sum or difference of terms.
-
-```gramaire
-Expr
-  : Expr '+' Term
-  | Expr '-' Term
-  | Term
-```
-````
-
-Reading the `gramaire` block:
-
-- `Expr` on its own line names the nonterminal; the `:` on the next line begins
-  its alternatives.
-- `|` separates alternatives — and it is the **only** separator. A line break
-  inside an alternative is insignificant, so a long alternative may wrap freely.
-- Quoted spellings like `'+'` (single or double quotes) are **literal
-  terminals** — the exact text to match.
-- A **mixed-case** name (`Expr`, `Term`) is a nonterminal; an **ALL-CAPS** name
-  (`NUMBER`) is a lexer token class. A mixed-case name you never define is a
-  missing rule — Gramaire rejects it by name rather than treating it as a phantom
-  terminal.
-
-<Aside type="caution" title="Heads vs. fields">
-  A rule head is `Name` on its own line, then `:` on the next — the line break
-  is load-bearing. It is the one thing that distinguishes a head from a
-  `name:Sym` **field** (written `IDENT : Sym` with no break, see §4). So never
-  write a head inline as `Name : …`.
-</Aside>
-
-Add the remaining rules — `Term`, then `Factor` for numbers and parentheses:
-
-```gramaire
-Term
-  : Term '*' Factor
-  | Term '/' Factor
-  | Factor
-
-Factor
-  : '(' Expr ')'
-  | NUMBER
-```
-
-`Factor` mentions the `NUMBER` token class but nothing has said what a `NUMBER`
-_is_ yet. Declare token classes in a reserved `## Tokens` section, each an
-ALL-CAPS name bound to a `/regex/`; mark throwaway classes (whitespace) `%skip`:
-
-````md
-## Tokens
-
-```gramaire tokens
-NUMBER : /[0-9]+/
-WS     : /[ \t\r\n]+/   %skip
-```
-````
-
-That is the whole recognizer's vocabulary. Gramaire renders each rule as a
-**railroad diagram** — the same SVGs `gramaire fmt` writes back into your
-`.gram.md`, so the committed file documents itself. Here is the calculator's
-shape, the stratification visible at a glance:
-
-<RuleDiagram grammar={getDefaultGrammar()} rule="Expr" />
-<RuleDiagram grammar={getDefaultGrammar()} rule="Term" />
-<RuleDiagram
-  grammar={getDefaultGrammar()}
-  rule="Factor"
-  caption="Expr, Term, and Factor — sums of products of atoms."
-/>
-
-A rule draws itself. Here is the smallest possible one — edit it and watch the
-railroad redraw. There is no input box, so there is no verdict: omit the input
-and a live editor is just a diagram of the grammar.
-
-<LiveGrammar grammar={DIGIT} caption="a rule draws itself — edit it" />
-
-We will run the calculator in §5; first, two conveniences.
-
-## 3. Surface sugar
-
-Writing pure, left-recursive, epsilon-free productions by hand is wordy.
-Gramaire gives you sugar that compiles down to that clean core automatically
-(`Gramaire.Desugar`), so the table generator never sees a nullable rule.
-
-<CardGrid>
-  <Card title="Repetition">
-    `X+` one-or-more, `X*` zero-or-more, `X?` optional. `X+` becomes a fresh
-    left-recursive list; `X*` and `X?` enumerate present/absent at the use site,
-    so the core stays epsilon-free.
-  </Card>
-  <Card title="Separated lists">
-    `Comma<X>` and `Sep<X, S>` expand to one-or-more lists separated by `,` or by
-    any symbol `S` — e.g. `'{' Comma<Member> '}'`.
-  </Card>
-  <Card title="Named fields">
-    `left:Expr` names a right-hand position. The name rides onto the IR
-    (`rhs[].field`) and drives generated CST accessors and visitors — without
-    changing the recognized language.
-  </Card>
-  <Card title="Inline folding">
-    `#[inline]` on a rule folds its single production into every use site, then
-    drops it — a DRY tool, and a way to hand-fit a grammar into LR(1).
-  </Card>
-</CardGrid>
-
-For example, a statement block is just:
-
-```gramaire
-Block
-  : '{' Sep<Stmt, ';'> '}'
-```
-
-## 4. Precedence and conflicts
-
-A <Term name="shift-reduce">shift/reduce conflict</Term> is what a recursive,
-ambiguous operator grammar produces. Declare operator precedence in a reserved
-section to resolve it — earlier declarations bind more loosely:
-
-````md
-## Precedence
-
-```gramaire precedence
-%left '+' '-'
-%left '*' '/'
-```
-````
-
-When a build _does_ conflict, Gramaire never tells you "conflict in state 7." It
-names the competing rules — "shift `+` vs reduce `Expr -> Expr + Expr`" — and it
-can tell you _what kind_ of conflict it is:
-
-- an **<Term name="lalr-artifact">LALR artifact</Term>** — canonical LR(1) or
-  IELR(1) resolves it, so just build with a stronger method;
-- **resolved by declaration** — your `%left`/`%right` lines already clear it, so
-  the grammar compiles as written; or
-- a **genuine** conflict — the grammar really is ambiguous or not LR(1) _even
-  with_ the declared precedence, and needs a refactor, another precedence rule,
-  or the GLR engine.
-
-```sh
-gramaire explain-conflict calc.gram.md
-```
-
-## 5. Run the recognizer
-
-That is a complete grammar — and as it stands it is a **recognizer**: it answers
-exactly one question, _does this input fit?_ Try it right here — edit either box
-and the real engine re-lexes, re-parses, and redraws live:
-
-<LiveGrammar grammar={CALC} input="2 + 3 * 4" />
-
-- `12 + 3 * 4` → **accepted**
-- `12 +` → **rejected** — a `Term` has to follow `+`
-
-This is the same Scala core the CLI runs — the `NUMBER` token class lexes
-client-side — so the verdict here is the verdict `gramaire` gives. Open it in the
-full Lab to see the parse tree, the trace, and the conflict analysis:
-
-<OpenInLab preset="calc" label="Open the calculator in the Lab ↗" />
-
-<Aside type="tip" title="A recognizer is already useful">
-  Linters, validators, and syntax highlighters often need nothing more than
-  yes/no. If that is all you want, you are done. The rest of this tutorial is
-  **Part 2** — turning an accepted parse into a value.
-</Aside>
-
-## 6. From recognition to a value
-
-A recognizer alone is already a complete grammar — with no actions at all it
-still fully defines the recognized language and the concrete syntax tree
-(CST) any backend can walk; that's what Section 5 just proved. To turn that
-CST into a value instead — a number, an AST — declare the language your
-actions are written in with a document-level `%lang`, then attach an
-**action** between `{%` and `%}`. This is exactly the grammar the live editor
-above already runs:
-
-```gramaire
-%lang javascript
-
-Expr
-  : Expr '+' Term   {% (c) => c.expr + c.term %}
-  | Expr '-' Term   {% (c) => c.expr - c.term %}
-  | Term
-```
-
-Without a declared `%lang`, `{% … %}` text is carried through as opaque,
-unexecuted payload — a grammar with actions but no declared language doesn't
-get an implicit interpreter.
-
-An action receives its children as a single **namedtuple** `c`: an array read
-by index (`c[0]`, `c[2]`), or by field for a named right-hand position
-(`c.term`). A position with no explicit `name:` is still auto-named by its
-symbol when that symbol occurs once in the rule — `Term` → `c.term`, `Expr` →
-`c.expr`.
-
-<Aside title="From CST to AST">
-  The parser first builds a <Term name="cst">concrete syntax tree</Term> — every
-  token it matched, the `+` and the parentheses included. Your actions project
-  that onto the value you actually want: `(c) => c.expr + c.term` keeps the two
-  operands and drops the `+`; `Factor : '(' Expr ')'` returns the inner
-  `Expr`'s value and drops both brackets (`(c) => c.expr`). Same recognized
-  language, a value instead of a tree.
-</Aside>
-
-If you name your fields, you can destructure instead of indexing:
-
-```gramaire
-Expr
-  : left:Expr '+' right:Term   {% ({ left, right }) => left + right %}
-```
-
-<Aside title="Actions are data, backends are consumers">
-  Actions are carried verbatim into the [IR](../../specs/ir-schema/); each
-  backend reads only the IR. The TypeScript backend, for instance, emits a
-  runnable parser and a typed Visitor over the CST without ever seeing your
-  Markdown.
-</Aside>
-
-## 7. Emit a parser
-
-At the CLI, check the file and emit artifacts from the same grammar:
-
-```sh
-# verify the file (structure, formatting, no conflicts)
-gramaire fmt calc.gram.md
-
-# emit artifacts from the same grammar
-gramaire emit --backend ebnf calc.gram.md   # W3C-style EBNF
-gramaire emit --backend ts   calc.gram.md   # a runnable TS parser + Visitor
-gramaire emit --backend ir   calc.gram.md   # the gramaire-ir JSON
-```
-
-`gramaire fmt` also writes the railroad diagrams and the FIRST/FOLLOW table back
-into the document, so the file you commit renders as complete documentation.
